NATIONAL STATEMENT BY THE MINISTER OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS OF MALAYSIA AT THE GENERAL DEBATE OF THE 81ST SESSION OF THE UNITED NATIONS GENERAL ASSEMBLY, NEW YORK, 26 SEPTEMBER 2026 Theme; “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation: A United Nations that Delivers for All” Distinguished Delegates, Ladies and Gentlemen,
1. I join others in congratulating my friend, His Excellency Dr. Khalilur Rahman, on his election as President of the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly.
2. You have Malaysia’s full support as you lead this Assembly through a period of profound global uncertainty.
3. Indeed, we are meeting at the most challenging time for the UN in many years.
GOV1
4. The world has become accustomed to crisis. Wars are escalating.
PSJ1
merged
Major-power rivalry is sharpening.
The international arms-control architecture is under strain.
PSJ4
New technologies are transforming societies faster than our institutions can adapt.
INN4
5. But perhaps the greatest danger is not any one crisis.
It is the growing belief that the international system cannot solve them.
6. That is the trust deficit confronting the UN today.
7. And Malaysia believes we must confront it openly and honestly.
Trust can only be restored through concrete action.
8. When international law means what it says.
PSJ5
And when the people of the world can look to this Hall, and believe that their voices still matter.
REF3
9. We must remember that the UN is not merely here for the aftermath of war, but to prevent war from taking place.
10. Yet too often, we respond only after disaster has arrived.
11. We count the dead. We deliver supplies.
HUM3
We rebuild what has been destroyed.
And then we wait for the next crisis.
12. This cannot be the future of multilateralism.
We must move from reaction to prevention.
13. And nowhere is that task more urgent than in Gaza.
SIT_ISR_PSE
14. Malaysia will not stand here and recite statistics that everyone in this Hall already knows.
We all know the scale of death in Gaza.
15. We know how many children, families, medics, aid workers, and journalists have been slaughtered.
16. We also know that Gaza represents the highest number of children made orphans, in a single conflict.
17. Malaysia, and many other Member States, have exhausted every effort in the pursuit of justice for Gaza.
18. We have consistently called for immediate ceasefire and unrestricted supply of aid.
19. We have supported humanitarian works in Palestine.
20. We have pushed for punitive action towards Israel.
21. And we have advocated for full Palestinian membership in this Hall.
22. And yet, again and again, the collective will of this Assembly has encountered the silencing effect of the veto.
REF2
23. Malaysia will speak plainly:
24. We are sick of it.
25. Nowhere is the need for reform more critical than in the Security Council.
Nowhere are the shortcomings of the UN more glaring than in the Security Council.
26. The exercise of the veto must be questioned and strongly challenged by every single member of this General Assembly.
Particularly in cases of crimes against humanity.
27. Resolution 76/262 has already created an accountability channel between the Council and this Assembly.
28. We must make full use of this Resolution as a launchpad for greater accountability regarding the use of the veto.
29. Expanding the Council's membership alone will not be enough to resolve its failures.
It is the veto that must be challenged, and it is the veto that must be abolished.
We must begin the work now.
30. There is still time to save the global order.
The paralysis of the Security Council will not be the paralysis of the UN.
31.It is fair to say that global trust in the UN's ability to deliver is at an all-time low.
32. This, in turn, demolishes trust in the very idea of the multilateral order.
33. The citizens we serve and represent are afraid, Excellencies.
34. They are watching the world order fragment.
35. They are witnessing the re-emergence of an arms race.
36. They have heard overt threats to use nuclear weapons.
37. And they are seeing their governments choose not to regulate A.I., and the many ways it is being abused, but instead give it more power.
INN1
38. In such chaotic times, the only way to course-correct is to rebuild trust in the power of pro-active governance and multilateralism.
39. Trust comes from the way in which we, as world leaders, can manage transformative forces.
40. For centuries, global power was concentrated in states.
But today, a new source of power has emerged.
41. A handful of private actors now control how billions of people communicate, work, transact, and consume information.
42. Artificial intelligence is changing how economies operate, how societies function, and how governments make decisions.
43. The opportunities are enormous.
But so are the risks.
44. We must therefore ask a simple question: Who governs the transformation?
45. Technology must serve humanity. Never the reverse.
46. And the answer cannot be that a small number of companies or countries decide the rules for everyone else.
47. The UN must continue to empower Global South countries, who are likely to be more greatly affected by unequitable A.I. development, to participate in global discussions on A.I.
INN2
48. The Global South cannot simply become a destination for data centres, while decisions about A.I. are made elsewhere.
49. We must be partners in innovation.
Not merely customers and markets.
And not merely destinations for investment.
50. Partners, involved in the decisions that will shape our future.
51. Equitable decision-making, and equitable development.
52. That means managing the enormous demands that tech infrastructure places on water, energy, land, and other resources, so that the benefits of A.I. can be shared more broadly, across borders.
CLI2
53. In our hyper-connected world today, indeed, very few things stay where they begin.
Technologies are rapidly shared, and they can just as rapidly disrupt.
Similarly, war can also travel beyond borders.
54. Across West Asia, escalating conflict threatens some of the world's most important routes for energy and trade, including the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandab.
ECO2
SIT_MEO
55. The consequences of conflict do not stop at these shores.
A family in Southeast Asia has no part in these disputes.
Yet that family still pays the price, when food, fuel, and cost of living rise.
CLI1
DEV3
DEV4
56. Malaysia therefore urges all parties to step back from escalation.
57. Diplomacy has shown that dialogue is possible.
That path must not be abandoned.
58. Or we risk sending further shockwaves through global markets, and needlessly bringing suffering to innocent families around the world.
59. Most nations in this Hall are not great powers.
Yet decisions taken by a few can shape the future of all.
60. We are the global majority.
As I said earlier, we must not simply live with the consequences of choices made elsewhere.
We must help shape those choices.
61. Middle powers, such as Malaysia, can help keep dialogue alive when major powers cannot agree.
62. Regional organisations, such as ASEAN, can bring the perspectives of their people into global debates.
We must have the confidence to speak for our regions, not be spoken for.
63. I began by speaking about trust.
Let me close where I began.
64. The question before us may appear simple, but in truth, it is profound.
65. When people are suffering, and when the world looks towards this Hall, will this organisation still answer the call for which it was created?
66. Actions speak louder than words, my esteemed Colleagues.
67. We must restore trust. Manage transformation.
68. Reform institutions that no longer serve current realities.
69. And we must ensure that the rules of the global system apply equally to all.
70. Malaysia will not turn away from the UN in its hour of difficulty.
We will not abandon multilateralism just because it is imperfect.
71. We will do the work, to make it worthy of the trust placed in it.
72. Because we believe in multilateralism, most of all, when the alternative is a world ruled by power alone.
73. Eighty years ago, the founders of this organisation resolved to save succeeding generations from war.
74. We are those succeeding generations.
And that promise now rests in our hands.
75. The world needs a UN that delivers.
76. One that ensures that international law is truly international.
And guarantees that every region has a voice.
77. And above all, one that ordinary people can look to in their darkest hour, and still believe that it will act.
That the world has not forgotten them.
78. Before concluding, we would like to offer our most heartfelt gratitude to Secretary General Antonio Guterres.
79. As this will be the final session of the General Assembly during his tenure, we thank him for leading the UN with unyielding dedication and patience through many unprecedented global upheavals.
80. These are the qualities we will need to face our future as an organisation.
81. And if there is anything that humanity has demonstrated throughout our history, it is our capacity to adapt.
82. My esteemed Colleagues, let us adapt and prove ourselves worthy of the promise entrusted to us.
Thank you.
